name: Triton
E_trait: retrograde orbit among moons >=1000 km (script's own 'every large moon' wording)
notes: Lost A2 and D5. Surface 230-320 Myr (up to 600-750 Myr on a shallower slope); only an under-estimated flux by ~6x reaches 40-50 Myr. Pressure unchanged 1989/2017/2022, no seasonal trend; the 1995-97 surge is ~2.5 sigma and the authors urge caution. D4=0: the Roadmap lists Triton as a candidate ocean world. Counter-source: Hansen 2021 PSJ, 'Likely Ocean World'. B5 SOURCED (abstract only): Chyba, Jankowski & Nicholson 1989, A&A 219, L23 - tides on both bodies spiral Triton inward; nominal parameters (obliquity state 1) reach Neptune's Roche limit in ~3.6 Gyr; state 2 ~1.4 Gyr. Weak: a pre-Voyager model, the timescale depends on assumed tidal Q/k2 (no measured decay rate), and the Cornell/Cassini-state-2 branch was later ruled out by Voyager. Wording used: 'billions of years, on current models', never a date. If B5 were 0, Triton = 15, still #4.

name: Enceladus
E_trait: confirmed water plumes from a subsurface ocean
notes: A2 confirmed: south polar terrain as young as 50 Myr, ridged plains ~70 Myr. Jet count (>100) is Porco 2014 and the hydrogen gas is Waite 2017 - neither is on NASA's Enceladus page.

name: Io
notes: NASA's Io page says 'hundreds of volcanoes' and gives no count; the ~400 figure is Lopes & Williams, not NASA. A4 confirmed by the new volcano JunoCam found in 2024 and absent from Galileo imagery.

name: Titan
notes: A2=0 confirmed: crater retention age 300-340 Myr with clathrates, 420 Myr without. A4 rests on the Ligeia Mare transient features (Hofgartner 2014) - the observation is solid, the mechanism is not. Surface pressure: Huygens ~1.45x Earth vs NASA's '60 percent greater'; the video uses one of the two.

name: Hyperion
notes: B2 is marginal: e=0.104-0.105 vs a 0.1 threshold, and PDS Rings lists 0.0232, which looks erroneous. The video does not rest its claim on '>0.1'. C3=0 is unverified either way. E=3 confirmed (Kerberos and Styx only suspected).

name: Janus & Epimetheus
E_trait: co-orbital pair that swaps orbits (pair counted as one unit)
notes: C1 dropped: Janus 1.31, Epimetheus 1.29, so not a majority. C4 is the strong flag (both ~0.64 g/cc). Epimetheus alone would score C2=1 (107/116 km = 0.92). NASA calls the swap the only such configuration known.

name: Ganymede
notes: Two judgment calls, both flagged. C3=0: dark ~0.2-0.25 vs bright ~0.35-0.44, about 2:1, fails 3:1. C5=0: grooved sulci terrain also occurs on Enceladus, Europa, Miranda and Ariel. E=1 is solid - NASA says it is the only moon with its own magnetic field.

name: Europa
E_trait: subsurface water ocean (confirmed/strongly supported): Europa, Ganymede, Titan, Enceladus, Mimas
notes: A2 straddles the threshold: NASA 40-90 Myr but Bierhaus 2013 gives 20-200 Myr. Wording used: 'tens of millions of years', not 'under 100 million'. A1=0: plumes still unconfirmed. C3=0 is a judgment call (lineae are a network, not a boundary). C5 uniqueness unsourced.

name: Iapetus
notes: C2 is robust via Turgis (580/1472 = 0.39); the ridge alone would be marginal (13 km measured vs 20 km model). Albedo 0.03-0.05 vs 0.5-0.6. The LEADING hemisphere is the dark one. Density 1.089 g/cc just misses the C4 cutoff.

name: Charon
notes: D5 dropped: Grundy 2016 is a model, and the mechanism converts volatiles to tholins rather than cycling them. Diameter ratio 0.510, i.e. just over half. B3 barycentre is derived, not directly cited. C2 marginal: chasms ~9 km vs the 10 km bar. B1=0 depends on the reference frame; the rubric states one.

name: Pan & Atlas
notes: No changes; all six flag values hold. Pan 17x16x10 km = 1.70, Atlas 20x18x9 km = 2.22. Densities 420 and 500 kg/m3 (NSSDC), far below 1.0 on every source. C5: ridges accreted from slow infall of ring material onto a tidally locked moonlet (Charnoz 2007) - Pan a sharp-edged ravioli polygon, Atlas a lens. Caveat: Iapetus also has an equatorial ridge but by a different route (fallback disk), so the claim is limited to a RING-ACCRETED ridge, not 'the only moons with an equatorial ridge'. C2 correctly 0: the ridges are only 6-8 km thick, under the 10 km bar. E=3 confirmed (Pan, Atlas, Daphnis); Daphnis carries two or three narrow ridges, the thinnest under 0.5 km, one near 22 deg N that may record a past tilt.

name: Mimas
E_trait: impact crater >=25% of body diameter (>=10 moons)
notes: Highest-risk row. A3 and D4 both rest on the SAME single 2024 Nature paper (Lainey et al., periapsis drift), which contradicts a still-live NASA page saying Mimas 'appears to be frozen solid'. Not independent evidence, so the video does not call the ocean 'confirmed'. Ocean younger than ~25 Myr; ice-ocean boundary above 30 km only in the last 2-3 Myr, which is why A2=0 and A5=0 are consistent. E=6 is a tabulation by the project; no published compilation exists, so the video says 'at least six'.

name: Miranda
notes: A5 raised to 1 on Strom et al. 2024 (PSJ): coronae stress patterns match tidal forcing 100-500 Myr ago. Single study. C2 dropped to 0: Thomas 1988 gives maximum deformation 'about 10 km', which is AT not above the >10 km bar, and no basin nears 25%. Verona Rupes best figures are 5-10 km (Thomas 1988) and 5-15 km corrected for oblique viewing (1991 LPSC); the 20 km figure often quoted comes from APOD, not a journal, and the video uses the journal range. The scarp runs past the terminator so its true height has no upper bound. Past ocean only (100-500 Myr ago), so D4 and A3 stay 0.

name: Nix & Hydra
notes: B4 is contested and is the weakest link. Showalter & Hamilton 2015 (Nature) say both rotate chaotically under Pluto-Charon torques. Weaver et al. 2016 (Science) measured well-determined periods (Nix 1.829 d, Hydra 0.4295 d) and concluded they have 'probably never reached the state of near-synchronicity' where chaos would dominate, explicitly deferring the question. The flag is kept only while citing Nature 2015, and the video says 'non-synchronous and fast'. Shapes solid: Nix 1.52, Hydra 2.60. C4 stays 0 - densities are undetermined, with mass errors up to ~100%.

name: Phobos
notes: A5 left at 0: two live competing groove models - Hurford 2016 matches the grooves to the present-day tidal stress field, Nayak & Asphaug attribute them to Mars impact-ejecta chains. A contested interpretation does not clear the bar; the same strictness is applied to Uranus's moons. B5 is the strongest flag: decaying ~2 m/century, disruption in 30-50 Myr (NASA) or 20-40 Myr (Black & Mittal 2015). C1 = 1.43. C2 carried by Stickney at 9-10 km on a 22.2 km body = 40-45%; the relief clause fails. C4 marginal: published porosity 25-45%, a range straddling the 30% bar, with 30+/-5% the midpoint - kept at 1 because '>=30%' includes 30. C3 and D1 are both unsourced either way, not measured as absent. E kept at 2 for internal consistency with Triton's B5.

name: Daphnis
notes: 4x source conflict on wave height: NASA says ~4 km from 2009 shadow lengths, the peer-reviewed 2024 Icarus N-body paper says ~1 km. The video never gives 4 km unqualified. 4.3x4.1x3.2 km gives ratio 1.34, just over the bar. Density 0.34 g/cc. E trait set to 'confirmed' waves: Pan's Encke Gap waves are confirmed but no height is published, so counting Pan avoids rewarding Daphnis for a gap in the literature rather than real rarity. C5 is class-level, shared with Pan and Atlas.

name: Phoebe
notes: C2 raised to 1: craters up to ~100 km on a ~213 km body = ~47%. C3 left at 0 despite a borderline case - Porco 2005 gives normal reflectance 0.07 to 0.30 (4.3:1, which would pass) but the same paper gives local albedo contrast factors of only 2.0-3.0. Two numbers in one source on opposite sides of the bar, so the conservative reading stands, consistent with Ganymede. B1 inclination 175.2 deg, B2 e=0.164, B4 rotation 9.27 h vs a ~550-day orbit. C1 stays 0 at 1.07. Retrograde count ~204 on current catalogues, but the Ashton 122-irregular total does not reconcile with Saturn's 274-292 moons; if the 2025 discoveries are overwhelmingly retrograde the real figure is ~320. The video says 'more than two hundred, probably over three hundred' and cites the catalogue date. The rarity score is 0 either way.

name: Methone
E_trait: crater-free surface among ring-embedded moonlets (Methone, Pallene, Aegaeon, Anthe)
notes: C1 raised to 1: 3.88x2.58x2.42 km = 1.60 (Thomas 2013). Crater-free is solid - imaged at 27 m/pixel from 4,000 km, no craters larger than 130 m. A2 stays 0: the 0.32 Gyr figure is a COLLISIONAL FORMATION age, not a crater-count surface age, and the smoothness is regolith mobility, not young emplacement. E raised to 4: Pallene, Aegaeon and Anthe are also crater-free, but at much worse resolution than Methone.

name: Uranus inner moons
E_trait: member of a dynamically unstable group predicted to collide within ~100 Myr (Portia group)
notes: Membership 13->14: S/2025 U1 found by JWST in Feb 2025. B3 holds for 9 of 14 (Cordelia 24:25 and Ophelia 14:13 shepherd the epsilon ring; Perdita, Cupid, Cressida, Juliet all near resonances). B5: the Portia group is unstable, Cressida-Desdemona first to collide, under ~100 Myr (Cuk 2022). Cuk 2022 reverses French & Showalter 2012 on the Belinda group, which is now stable over 50 Myr. E set to 6 (the whole unstable Portia group) rather than 2 (just the colliding pair); the narrower reading would add 4 points. No axis-ratio measurement exists for any of these bodies, so C1=0 is unsourced rather than measured.

name: Irregular captured moons
notes: C1 dropped to 0: no shape determination exists for the overwhelming majority, and the best-measured irregular, Phoebe, is a flattened spheroid at a/c ~1.08, not elongated. B1 holds: 100 of 122 Saturnian irregulars are retrograde Norse-group members and the 128 added in 2025 concentrate in the retrograde Mundilfari subgroup. B2 holds: only ~3 of 122 have e <= 0.1. Count ~375, derived as sourced per-planet totals minus regular satellites; no catalogue publishes an irregular total. Per-planet totals used at the time of scoring: Jupiter 115, Saturn 274, Uranus 29, Neptune 16.

name: Uranus big four
notes: D4 and A3 left at 0 under a rule applied consistently across the table: the ocean flag requires evidence from spacecraft measurements (induced field, gravity/libration, astrometry or plume sampling). Castillo-Rogez 2023 models all four as likely retaining oceans, warmest for Titania and Oberon, but it is thermal-evolution modelling with no detection - confirmation needs a magnetometer. The same rule keeps Triton, Miranda and Dione at 0. A5=0: Ariel's young regions are 1-2 Ga, which fails the ~1 Gyr bar, and 1 of 4 is not a majority. C2=0: only Oberon qualifies, via an ~11 km limb mountain; the largest craters reach just 14-21% of body diameter. All four are in no mean-motion resonances. Polar-night wording: NASA says each pole gets 'nearly a quarter of each Uranian year' of sunlight and a '21-year-long, dark winter', on an 84-year orbit at 97.77 degrees tilt. The 42-year figure is half the orbit, solstice to solstice, not a NASA number. This is a definitional difference, not a factual one.

name: Amalthea
notes: The most fragile row in the table. C4 rests on Anderson et al. 2005 Science, titled 'Amalthea's Density Is Less Than That of Water', at 857 +/- 99 kg/m3 - but JPL SSD currently lists 1.0111 +/- 0.1213 g/cc, i.e. above water. The two agree within mutual 1 sigma so neither is refuted. Flag kept at 1; the video says 'about the density of water, possibly below it', never 'less dense than water' as settled. C2 dropped to 0: NASA confirms a large south-polar crater (Gaea) but publishes no diameter, and the ~80-100 km figures could not be sourced. E corrected 10 -> 17: sub-water density is common (Helene 0.292, Daphnis 0.340, Pan, Atlas, Prometheus, Pandora, Hyperion, Epimetheus, Janus, even Tethys at 0.985, plus Metis, Adrastea, Thebe, Himalia, Nix). Amalthea is the least secure member of a list of 17, so this is a weak signature trait for it.

name: Callisto
notes: D4=1 now has a second, stronger source than the Roadmap: Cochrane et al. 2025 (AGU Advances) reanalysed all eight Galileo close flybys and found an ionosphere alone cannot reproduce the induction signal. Caveat: NASA's own Callisto page has not caught up and still says the ocean 'may be deeper than thought or may not exist', and a Nov 2025 review calls it uncertain. Wording used: 'strongly supported, not confirmed - JUICE and Europa Clipper will settle it'. A3 left at 0 deliberately: Callisto is outside the Laplace resonance with negligible tidal dissipation, and flipping it would make A3 a duplicate of D4 for every ocean world. C2 depends on definition by a factor of 6: Valhalla's central bright basin is 600 km (12.5%, fails) but the full multi-ring structure is ~4,000 km (83%, passes). Kept at 1 under the rule that the catalogued structure diameter counts, the same basis as South Pole-Aitken for the Moon. E corrected 10 -> 14; a >4 Gyr surface is not rare. An alternative trait is 'most crater-saturated surface in the solar system', which NASA states for Callisto and which would give N=1.

name: Tethys, Dione, Rhea
notes: C2 raised to 1: Odysseus 400 km on a ~1,066 km Tethys = 38%, and Evander 350 km on a ~1,124 km Dione = 31%, so 2 of 3 clear the bar. Rhea misses, with Tirawa at 360/1,528 = 24%. Relief fails separately - Ithaca Chasma is only 3-5 km deep. D1 holds for 2 of 3: Rhea's O2/CO2 exosphere is Cassini-confirmed and Dione's sputter-produced O2+ exosphere is confirmed by CAPS; Tethys has no bound-exosphere detection. Trojans: Tethys has Telesto and Calypso, Dione has Helene and Polydeuces, Rhea has NONE. RUBRIC RULE APPLIED: Trojan companions are companions, not group members - if they were members the group would be 7 bodies, C1 would flip to 1 and C2 back to 0. Dione's own ocean (Beuthe 2016, ice shell 99+/-23 km over a 65+/-30 km ocean) qualifies individually but is 1 of 3, so the group ocean flag stays 0.

name: Nereid
notes: B4 raised to 1: rotation period 11.594 +/- 0.017 h (Kepler/K2) against a ~360-day orbit, emphatically non-synchronous. E=1 CONFIRMED and genuinely alone - the irregular-satellite catalogues were checked and nothing comes close: Saturn tops out at 0.625, Jupiter at 0.437 (Aoede), the Uranian Sycorax group at 0.52, and Neptune's next-highest is Psamathe at 0.45. C1 stays 0 with a real source now: light-curve amplitudes cap the axis ratio at ~1.3:1, which EXCLUDES the older 1.9:1 elongated shape. B3 stays 0 - Belyakov 2026 argues Nereid was scattered by Triton's capture, a past event, not a current resonance.

name: Hippocamp
E_trait: published impact-fragment origin hypothesis (no source enumerates a count)
notes: All 20 flags correctly 0, but most C and D zeros reflect absence of data, not measurement - it has never been resolved. The video says 'unknown', not 'no'. Showalter et al. 2019 concludes only that it is 'probably an ancient fragment of Proteus', from orbital proximity (semimajor axes differ by 10%) plus Proteus's tidal migration. The Pharos crater link in popular coverage is not in the paper's abstract. E trait is the weakest in the table: impact-fragment origin is a hypothesis class, not an observable, and no source enumerates a count.

name: Moon
notes: A5 raised to 1: thousands of young lobate thrust scarps in LROC, and 8 of 28 Apollo shallow moonquakes within 30 km of mapped faults (Watters 2010, 2019). A4 strong: >200 new impact craters and >47,000 surface 'splotches' during the LRO mission (Speyerer 2016). C2 strong both ways: South Pole-Aitken is 2400x2050 km against a 3475 km diameter, i.e. 69%. A3 left at 0 by definition: Weber 2011 supports a fluid metallic outer core, but this rubric reads 'liquid layer' as water or silicate melt sustained by ongoing heating, not a residual metallic core. A2 left at 0: Braden 2014 dates three irregular mare patches to <100 Myr, but it is disputed and covers a few square km. E=4 only if restricted to planets and dwarf planets (Earth 1.23%, Pluto ~12%, Orcus 5-20%, Eris 0.87-2.7% straddling the bar); the video states that restriction on screen, since unrestricted it is dozens.

name: Deimos
E_trait: regolith ponding / crater infill (Deimos, Telesto, Calypso, Helene)
notes: C4 raised to 1: density 1.48 +/- 0.22 g/cc implies 40-60% porosity (Rosenblatt 2011); caveat, some of that may be water ice rather than void. C2 left at 0 pending the primary source: Raducan et al. 2026 Nature Astronomy describes a south-polar depression but the official release gives no dimensions; the ~10 km figure (which would be 67-81% of the body and would flip C2 to 1) is secondary coverage only. Named craters do not qualify - the largest is Voltaire at 2.3 km. E trait has a published basis: Thomas 2013 documents crater filling and ponding on Telesto, Calypso and Helene.

name: Dwarf-planet moons
notes: Count of moons of dwarf planets, asteroids and trans-Neptunian objects, kept at 470 for scoring. Dated figure: NASA Moons facts page, 'As of March 25, 2025 ... More than 470 confirmed moons orbiting other officially confirmed dwarf planets, asteroids and trans-Neptunian objects' (Wayback Machine snapshot of 2025-06-05). Johnston's Archive (page dated 30 Mar 2025) lists 597 moons of dwarf planets, asteroids and outer solar system objects (9 + 449 + 139), a wider tally that includes unconfirmed objects, so it is context and not a source for 470. NASA's current page says only 'Hundreds of other moons', so the video says 'hundreds'. Charon is scored separately and NASA counts it inside Pluto's 5 in the planetary total, so there is no double-count. All-zero is defensible but rests on the absence of published measurements; the video says 'unmeasured', not 'absent'. Dysnomia justifies no flag: e<0.004, no shape and no measured density.
